evidence_items.summary: CIM-QA is a comprehensive, YAML-based evaluation benchmark designed to assess the performance of the CIMon agent in navigating and querying Common Information Model (CIM) ontologies. The dataset evaluates the agent's ability to translate natural language questions into complex graph traversals and time-series data retrievals. It is structured around distinct graph patterns, or templates, which range in structural complexity from 0 to 4 "hops" (property traversals). These templates require the resolution of various entity identifiers (e.g., name, rdfs:label, mRID, significantMrid, EIC code) as well as the application of literal constraints and filters (e.g., rated voltage, start dates). Dataset Composition: The dataset comprises two main components spanning varying levels of complexity: Knowledge Graph (KG) Dataset: 2,508 templates and 5,204 unique parameterised questions requiring 0 to 4 hops across the CIM knowledge graph. Time-Series Dataset: 6 templates and 60 questions that evaluate the agent's ability to fuse CIM model data with dynamic time-series observations retrieved from the Cognite Data Fusion platform. Technical Structure: Each YAML entry in the dataset operates as a structured evaluation template encompassing: Natural Language Questions: Up to five varied question formulations per structural pattern. Parameters & Filters: Defined graph paths, CIM types, and literal constraints required to successfully construct the query. Parameterised SPARQL Templates & Bindings: The underlying SPARQL query patterns and specific IRI mappings for each question. Expected Agent Trajectories: Ordered groups of reference steps (e.g., iri discovery, sparql query, Retrieve Time Series, Retrieve Datapoints) that define the expected tool calls and input arguments. This includes expected SPARQL result sets for deterministic accuracy evaluation of the CIMon agent. Dependencies & Base Models: This repository provides the evaluation dataset only.
evidence_items.title: CIM-QA: A Benchmark Question-Answering Dataset for Agent Evaluation over the CIM Ontology and Time-Series Data

evidence_items.summary: "The RS-SynAgent Benchmark Dataset is an expert-defined benchmark designed to evaluate the planning and execution capabilities of large language model (LLM)-based agents in complex remote sensing workflows. The dataset comprises 755 benchmark tasks, including 455 single-tool tasks and 300 multi-tool tasks. It integrates structured task descriptions, remote sensing input data, expert-defined reference workflows, parameter configurations, and associated reference data to support systematic evaluation of tool selection, parameter configuration, multi-step workflow planning, and execution reliability.The dataset is organized into task-level benchmark information, remote sensing input resources, and reference data. The input resources include geospatial raster imagery in GeoTIFF format, organized into multiple batches, while the reference data provide supporting information for task execution and evaluation. The dataset does not include precomputed processing-result files; instead, users can generate processing outputs by executing the corresponding remote sensing workflows.Associated with the RS-SynAgent framework, this benchmark provides a structured resource for evaluating knowledge-constrained tool use and collaborative multi-tool execution. It aims to facilitate reproducible experiments, comparative evaluation, and further research on reliable intelligent agents for remote sensing and Earth observation applications."

evidence_items.summary: Detectors can flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from the traces of the tools they call. In the eleven evaluations we audited, attacks or anomalies make up 16% to 86% of the test samples, no evaluation varies that share, and six report no test on data from a second benchmark or source. We ask what such evaluations hide. On the AgentDrift and AgentDojo benchmarks we test trained detectors that read tool identities, behavior, call sequences, step embeddings or text, and a released LLM action monitor, AlignmentCheck, with thresholds fixed on training data or set by the monitor's released decision rule. First, at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.879 reaches a precision of 0.076, and the mix of negatives alone moves that precision between 0.039 and 0.117. Second, as tool coverage, the share of test tool calls whose tool was seen in training, falls, detector rankings cross near 50% coverage and reverse below it, because unseen tools map to inputs that training never reached. Dropout on tool inputs largely removes the reversal. Third, no detector trained on AgentDrift ranks AgentDojo traces better than chance (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52), including one that reaches 0.996 within AgentDojo. The monitor, trained on neither, reaches 0.930, but with its open backbone its released decision rule would still mostly raise false alerts at a 2% attack rate (precision 0.096). We turn these findings into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.
evidence_items.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for technical tasks in the oil and gas industry. Well-log interpretation requires combining depth-indexed measurements, derived petrophysical properties, and quality-control information to characterize lithology, porosity, permeability, fluid saturation, and reservoir quality within intervals and across formations and wells. Reliable interpretation depends on cross-curve consistency, data quality, and the availability of complementary measurements. Recent work introduced WellLogBench and WellLog-LLM (Shikhar, S. et al., 2026) to provide such a reproducible evaluation setting. WellLogBench established an expert-validated benchmark based on public LAS data and structured petrophysical contexts. These contexts are constructed using Petrophys (Shikhar, S. et al., 2026), an open-source library for standardized well-log processing, normalization, derivation of petrophysical properties, and assembly of model-ready interpretation contexts. WellLog-LLM combines Dynamic Feature Selection with supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and Group Relative Context Optimization (GRCO). GRCO is a training-free, GRPO-inspired method that derives reusable guidance from relative comparisons of model rollouts and applies it during inference without updating model weights. Although the aforementioned work provides a reproducible setting for well-log reasoning, its scope does not cover the full conditions encountered in operational carbonate fields. Operational carbonate datasets contain operator-specific mnemonics, incomplete log suites, logs from different vintages and acquisition types (e.g., wireline and LWD), borehole and acquisition effects, legacy interpreted curves, and sparse core coverage. Models must distinguish direct measurements from derived properties and qualify their conclusions when the required evidence is absent.
evidence_items.title: Well-Log LLM Benchmark: The First ADNOC Domain-Expert Curated Benchmark for LLM Reasoning of Well Logs on Carbonate Reservoirs

evidence_items.summary: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI ( 100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
evidence_items.title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning has accelerated automated atomic model building from cryo-EM maps, yet progress remains limited by the lack of large, high-quality datasets and standardized evaluation benchmarks. We address this gap by introducing CryoAtlas, a rigorously curated dataset and unified benchmark for density-guided atomic model building of protein chains. By integrating and filtering EMDB and PDB entries (up to March 2026), CryoAtlas provides 17,809 map-model-sequence entries, including a curated 16,657-entry training split. From this resource, we construct a 618-target benchmark with a shared evaluation protocol that jointly assesses structural accuracy, model-to-map fit, and stereochemical validity. Using this framework, we benchmark state-of-the-art learning-based methods against Phenix and AlphaFold3, comprehensively analyzing the impact of map resolution, sequence length, protein category and sequence identity on modeling accuracy. As a case study, retraining the ModelAngelo CNN component on CryoAtlas improves performance on the benchmark. CryoAtlas provides an open, reproducible foundation for future cryo-EM atomic model building research. Project details and resource release updates are available at https://oulling.github.io/cryoatlas/.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Formation evaluation is an investigation, not a single calculation or chat response. A petrophysicist must establish data readiness, select methods that fit the rock and available logs, compare several measurements, record uncertain inputs, and revise the interpretation when evidence conflicts. This paper presents PetroHarness, a harness designed for human supervision and open-source release that organizes this work around deterministic petrophysical calculations and a retained review package. PetroHarness separates scientific calculation from language-model coordination. The existing Petrophys library performs the depth-wise calculations. PetroHarness resolves the formation, checks inputs, builds a dependency-ordered scientific state, and lets a bounded LLM investigator request task-specific evidence through registered operations. Candidate reports are checked against the scientific results available to the model. The selected report, operation trace, evidence contract, and selection record are retained for petrophysicist review. The system was compared with a Baseline Agent using the same well logs, formation context, language model, Petrophys library (Shikhar et al. 2026), questions, and evaluator. In an automated benchmark-development evaluation of 221 questions from 18 wells and 50 formations, a content-centered Answer Quality Score increased from 38.82 to 52.02. The paired gain was 13.20 points, with a well-level 95% bootstrap interval of 10.14 to 16.31, and scores increased in every task family, with 180 of 221 cases improving. PetroHarness retained a portable trace, evidence contract, and draft-selection record for every run. Among reports containing numbers, at least 95% of the reported values could be found in the saved calculations in 98.6% of PetroHarness reports, compared with 12.0% for the Baseline Agent. The contribution is a practical boundary for agentic subsurface work.
evidence_items.title: PetroHarness: An Open-Source Agentic Harness for Auditable Formation Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Traditional robot task planning struggles to recover from failures and changing requirements because it relies on predefined rules, labelled datasets, and limited state awareness. Digital twins provide real-time virtual representations of physical systems, while multi-agent systems support collaborative, stepwise reasoning. However, their integration for failure evaluation, requirement adaptation, and state-aware robot planning remains underexplored, particularly at the architectural level. This study proposes a multi-agentic digital twin framework for human-in-the-loop workflows, enabling bidirectional communication between machines, digital twins, and multi-agents. The framework is validated through robot task planning for an aerospace product-qualification metrology process. Results show that digital-twin integration adds 885-1,149 milliseconds to communication between robots and agents because continuous state updates are required. Multi-agent workflows need more human feedback than single-agent workflows to align outputs with predefined goals and mitigate hallucinations, highlighting the importance of human-in-the-loop orchestration. Datasets, logs, code, videos, results, and deployment instructions are available on GitHub 1 .
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Agentic Digital Twin Framework for Human-in-the-loop Workflows

evidence_items.summary: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.
evidence_items.title: Think in 360{\deg}: Benchmarking and Bootstrapping Panoramic Video Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.
evidence_items.title: GraphNIAH: A Benchmark for Long-Context Reasoning over Real-World Graphs

evidence_items.summary: We present Ax-Prover, a multi-agent system for automated theorem proving in Lean that can solve problems across diverse scientific domains and operate either autonomously or collaboratively with human experts. To achieve this, Ax-Prover approaches scientific problem solving through formal proof generation, a process that demands both creative reasoning and strict syntactic rigor. Ax-Prover meets this challenge by equipping Large Language Models (LLMs), which provide knowledge and reasoning, with Lean tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which ensure formal correctness. To evaluate its performance as an autonomous prover, we benchmark our approach against frontier LLMs and specialized prover models on two public math benchmarks and on two Lean benchmarks we introduce in the fields of abstract algebra and quantum theory. On public datasets, Ax-Prover is competitive with state-of-the-art provers, while it largely outperforms them on the new benchmarks. This shows that, unlike specialized systems that struggle to generalize, our tool-based agentic theorem prover approach offers a generalizable methodology for formal verification across diverse scientific domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate Ax-Prover's assistant capabilities in a practical use case, showing how it enabled an expert mathematician to formalize the proof of a complex cryptography theorem.
evidence_items.title: Ax-Prover: A Deep Reasoning Agentic Framework for Theorem Proving in Mathematics and Quantum Physics

evidence_items.summary: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.
evidence_items.title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI

evidence_items.summary: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.
evidence_items.title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language compositionality is the ability to identify which properties, relations, quantities, and states bind to which entities in both an image and a caption, and to match those bindings across modalities. Existing benchmarks evaluate this ability through image-text matching: a model ranks candidate image-caption match similarities and succeeds when the correct match comes on top. In such datasets, paired images differ by more than a single binding: scene, layout, and content all differ, with 97% of pixels changing on average. Such pairs do not isolate compositionality: results are confounded by global image differences. We introduce Compositional Single-EdiT (CompoSET), a benchmark dataset in which each base image-caption pair has an edited counterpart, or foil, that preserves the scene but differs by a single controlled edit, such as color, count, spatial relation, or object state. Base and foil images preserve naturalistic scene complexity yet are visually near-identical: only 8% of pixels change on average. Our dataset has many foils per base scene (~22) in order to separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty, a distinction one-foil-per-base benchmarks cannot make. CompoSET contains 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, spanning 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, with captions at 3 verbosity levels. We test 22 dual-encoder VLMs and find that all models perform at or below chance level on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks. This suggests that apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact arising from confounds in benchmark design, and that compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved. CompoSET addresses the confounds and offers a better controlled benchmark to measure future progress.
evidence_items.title: CompoSET: A Controlled Single-Edit Benchmark for Vision-Language Compositionality

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for personal tasks, yet evaluating their safe use of personal context remains difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic, and socially situated. We introduce P-ContextBench, a realistic, verifiable, and scalable benchmark for evaluating personal-context understanding. P-ContextBench constructs population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans from demographic seeds reflecting the U.S. population. Rather than using explicit, static profiles, P-ContextBench embeds traits, routines, goals, and constraints as implicit evidence across fragmented, evolving synthetic mobile-app records. It evaluates five capabilities: single-source fact recovery, multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level personal patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests conflicting with persona-specific constraints through compliance, warning, clarification, or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, context recoverability, information leakage, evidence preservation, test-case grounding, and human-judge agreement. We instantiate P-ContextBench with 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments, and 4,810 verified test cases. The pipeline supports configurable generation across scales and demographic groups. Cost-effective state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs relevant to personal agents achieve below 60% accuracy on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference, and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions, with fewer than 10% of test cases answered correctly across all three repeated runs. Even a high-performing SOTA model remains inconsistent on these capabilities. P-ContextBench provides measurable targets for improving the accuracy, reliability, and safety of LLM-based personal agents.
evidence_items.title: P-ContextBench: From Personal Fact Recall to Personalized Agent Behavior

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
evidence_items.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness

evidence_items.summary: Foundation models for predictive machine learning on tabular data have recently gained significant traction in academia and industry. Research communities across disciplines are increasingly evaluating tabular foundation models on diverse datasets and tasks. However, these task- and discipline-specific evaluations remain largely inaccessible to model researchers because benchmark software and evaluation protocols are fragmented. As a result, model researchers rely on standard benchmarks, which are mostly defined for tasks where tabular foundation models already excel. The most challenging scenarios are excluded, limiting meaningful progress in the field by focusing on marginal improvements on IID data rather than on broader, more demanding challenges. To overcome this, we introduce BeyondArena, the first unified holistic benchmark for tabular data that supports diverse task types (IID, temporal, grouped), across sample size and feature dimensionality scales, with diverse feature types (with text, with high cardinality) from a broad range of disciplines. To enable unified benchmarking beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce DataFoundry, a Python framework and metadata schema for curating tabular datasets for predictive machine learning. Our results across 11 models and 142 curated datasets show that current open-source tabular foundation models are competitive or excel on datasets up to 100k rows, while traditional tree-based and deep learning models still dominate on grouped or large data. BeyondArena guides model research for the most demanding challenges in tabular data, enabling progress towards truly foundational tabular models.
evidence_items.title: Beyond IID: How General Are Tabular Foundation Models, Really?

evidence_items.summary: Preprint — critical narrative review; not peer reviewed. Machine learning studies report strong performance on fraudulent job advertisements, but benchmark scores alone provide limited evidence of reliable recruitment screening. This critical narrative review examines 13 purposively selected empirical studies published between 2017 and 2026, alongside dataset documentation and methodological literature. Ten core studies have explicitly identified ancestry in the Employment Scam Aegean Dataset; corpus cleaning, translation, and renaming therefore require provenance checks before being interpreted as independent validation. Reported results also differ in test populations, resampling boundaries, and metric averaging. A within-study resampling comparison illustrates how protocol changes alter the interpretation of accuracy, while recent cascades show that threshold adjustment and routing errors must be separated from the contribution of a second model. Contextual and human-input approaches broaden the available evidence, but subjective trust and predictive accuracy answer different questions. The review provides a study-level protocol audit and a reporting framework covering split independence, fraud-class performance, calibration, explanations, and operational outcomes. Priorities include independently collected multilingual advertisements, threshold-matched comparisons, and prospective assessment of human decisions. The resulting synthesis supports more informative evaluation rather than a ranking of architectures across incompatible experiments. Supporting materials: study-level evidence ledger, protocol audit, reference-verification record, search and evidence log, and LaTeX manuscript source. The core evidence includes 10 full-text appraisals and 3 appraisals limited to abstracts and publication records. AI assistance disclosure: This review develops an earlier university-project manuscript supplied by the author.
evidence_items.title: Learning to Detect Recruitment Fraud: A Critical Review of Dataset Lineage, Evaluation, and Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360° multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360° multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. evidence_items.summary: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

evidence_items.summary: In recent years, open-source efforts like Senorita-2M have propelled video editing toward natural language instruction. However, current publicly available datasets predominantly focus on local editing or style transfer, which largely preserve the original scene structure and are easier to scale. In contrast, Background Replacement, a task central to creative applications such as film production and advertising, requires synthesizing entirely new, temporally consistent scenes while maintaining accurate foreground-background interactions, making large-scale data generation significantly more challenging. Consequently, this complex task remains largely underexplored due to a scarcity of high-quality training data. This gap is evident in poorly performing state-of-the-art models, e.g., Kiwi-Edit, because the primary open-source dataset that contains this task, i.e., OpenVE-3M, frequently produces static, unnatural backgrounds. In this paper, we trace this quality degradation to a lack of precise background guidance during data synthesis. Accordingly, we design a scalable pipeline that generates foreground and background guidance in a decoupled manner with strict quality filtering. Building on this pipeline, we introduce Sparkle, a dataset of ~140K video pairs spanning five common background-change themes, alongside Sparkle-Bench, the largest evaluation benchmark tailored for background replacement to date. Experiments demonstrate that our dataset and the model trained on it achieve substantially better performance than all existing baselines on both OpenVE-Bench and Sparkle-Bench. Our proposed dataset, benchmark, model, as well as the full data generation pipeline, are fully open-sourced at https://showlab.github.io/Sparkle/.
evidence_items.title: Sparkle: Realizing Lively Instruction-Guided Video Background Replacement via Decoupled Guidance

evidence_items.summary: Purpose Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context. Findings Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning. Practical implications The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process. Originality/value By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.
evidence_items.title: Large language models in geospatial science

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) faces a hard constraint in public-facing nutri-tion QA: answers must be faithful to official sources. Yet Chinese official nutrition data lacks an auditable evaluation benchmark —numeric faithfulness, refusal bound-aries, and hallucination suppression remain unquantified. We present NutriQA, a traceable RAG question-answering benchmark on official Chinese nutrition data: 200 items in a four-category taxonomy (composition 60 / guideline 50 / special 50 / re-fusal 40), a three-level gold-provenance system (official food-composition values, ver-batim guideline excerpts, gold-free refusal items), and fully auditable deterministic judgment rules (numeric ±1 tolerance + key-point coverage + fabrication detection). Full-scale experiments on three commercial models (qwen-plus, deepseek-chat, glm-5.3-flash) show: (1) hybrid retrieval (BM25 character-bigram + vector RRF, top k=8) achieves a 160/160 hit rate, with retrieval method choice outweighing chunking gran-ularity; (2) retrieval optimization lifts RAG gain from ~0.15–0.17 to 0.20–0.225, de-coupling retrieval hit from the generator; (3) a novel boundary subclass (out-of-KB foods × numeric baits) quantifies 100% numeric fabrication by bare LLMs over out-of-KB objects with mutually exclusive cross-model intervals (3–4× apart), which RAG compresses to ~0–2.5% via“retrieved-not-covered → refuse”; (4) deterministic rules agree with human annotation at 0.949, outperforming a generic LLM judge at 0.846. Data, code, and full evidence are pinned at git tag v1.0.0 for independent verification and reproduction.
evidence_items.title: NutriQA: A Traceable RAG Question-Answering Benchmark and Empirical Study on Official Chinese Nutrition Data

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The drilling industry continues to pursue technologies that improve operational efficiency while reducing environmental impact and health, safety, and environmental risks. Conventional logging-while-drilling (LWD), measurement-while-drilling (MWD), and rotary steerable system (RSS) bottomhole assemblies (BHAs) rely on lithium batteries to power downhole electronics, introducing limitations associated with battery capacity, transportation, handling, replacement, and disposal. This paper presents the first successful global deployment of a fully battery-less triple-combo RSS BHA in a horizontal carbonate reservoir in North Oman. The system replaced conventional lithium battery modules with a mud-driven turbine-generator architecture capable of continuously supplying electrical power to the RSS, MWD telemetry, and triple-combo LWD sensors. The BHA acquired real-time azimuthal gamma ray, resistivity, density, neutron porosity, and directional measurements while maintaining continuous steering performance throughout the drilling interval. The field deployment demonstrated uninterrupted power generation, stable telemetry performance, continuous high-quality formation evaluation, and successful trajectory control without battery replacement or power interruption. The elimination of lithium batteries reduced operational complexity, hazardous material handling, logistics requirements, and environmental footprint while maintaining drilling performance comparable to conventional battery-powered systems. The successful implementation establishes a new benchmark for sustainable downhole power management and demonstrates the technical readiness of battery-less drilling systems for future global deployment.
evidence_items.title: New Benchmark for Battery-Less Drilling Technologies: First Trial in North Oman

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Building surrogate models for production system simulators is a recurring engineering task that remains manual, expert-dependent, and inconsistent across teams. Each update cycle requires a specialist to select input parameters, run simulations, choose ML architectures, tune hyperparameters, validate results, and package the model, spanning days to weeks. Conventional AutoML partially automates model selection but wastes resources on architectures more complex than necessary. This paper presents a multi-agent framework, powered by large language models (LLMs), that automates the full surrogate modelling lifecycle for multiphase production systems in two operating modes: conversational (expert-in-the-loop) and autonomous (self-optimizing until convergence). The framework makes four contributions. First, an autonomous Dataset Generation pipeline, which consists of a three-agent DAG (Sampling Designer, Simulation Runner, Data Reporter) that infers the relevant input parameters, their physically bounded ranges, and an appropriate Latin Hypercube sample size directly from a natural-language description of the well, dispatches the resulting design to the simulator, and returns an audited, reported dataset, removing the manual setup and scripting that otherwise precede every development cycle. Second, a complexity-aware experiment planning strategy in which every autonomous round starts from a default roster of fast, classical regressors spanning a linear, a kernel, and an ensemble-tree family, and escalates to deep-learning or gradient-boosted architectures only through the refinement loop, when a round's best result has failed to meet the stopping criterion. This eliminates the principal inefficiency of conventional AutoML, which is unnecessary evaluation of heavy models.
evidence_items.title: Production Surrogate Modelling Auto-Research Multi-Agentic System

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Offshore maintenance strategies for reciprocating engine-driven Booster Compressor (BC) packages rely heavily on static calendar intervals. This approach stems from fragmented technician logs, non-standardized field descriptions, and sparse failure records that hinder classical Weibull analysis. We addressed these data gaps across 51 satellite Wellhead Platforms (WHPs) in the Gulf of Thailand by deploying a digital reliability pipeline that combines Large Language Model (LLM) field log parsing, CMMS major overhaul synchronization, and hybrid Weibull-Exponential failure modeling. The framework was evaluated across 51 offshore Wellhead Platforms (WHPs) operating in the Gulf of Thailand, ingesting 711 historical shutdown records and mapping them against 114 predefined engineering risk categories using Large Language Models. To achieve high semantic precision, a domain-specific prompt architecture was engineered incorporating a field-jargon-to-engineering translation dictionary, exact predefined failure list injection, strict output constraints, zero-temperature generation control, and Python-level validation. Time-Between-Failures (TBF) datasets were systematically constructed by establishing platform-specific "Day 0" baselines from CMMS 48,000-hour major overhaul completion dates. Probabilistic failure behavior was quantified using a hybrid modeling structure: sparse failure modes (n = 2) were assigned a forced Exponential model (β=1.0), while modes with were fitted using Weibull Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). Lifecycle cost-rate optimization based on Nakagawa's age-replacement formulation was applied to 31 eligible failure modes with valid cost data. Time-based preventive maintenance (PM) proved cost-effective only for clear wear-out mechanisms (β &gt; 1), reducing lifecycle cost rates by up to 99.6% against run-to-failure (RTF). For random failure mechanisms (β ≈ 1) and sparse n=2 modes, calendar replacement yielded zero financial benefit.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Decision-Loop Asset Strategy Optimization Using Hybrid Probabilistic Failure Modeling

organizations: Institute for Advanced Study in Physics
evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents can coordinate computational drug discovery, but adapting a campaign to new evidence requires scientific software that supports flexible workflows, consistent modeling, and continuity across research sessions. Here we present ETALON, a harness that equips a general-purpose coding agent with an integrated environment for computer-aided drug design. Three independently usable systems supply its scientific operations: MolQuarry for chemical and biological evidence, MolCascade for molecular preparation, screening, and docking, and PRISM for molecular generation and physical modeling. Each exposes configurable procedures with explicit scientific requirements, so the host can revise its research strategy while retaining consistent preparation and evaluation practices. Operations registered with a common execution layer are checked before dispatch, and their outputs carry separate records of completion, verification, and admission, so that an incomplete computation is not recorded as an unfavorable molecular result. A persistent research graph links evidence, judgments, experiments, and results across sessions, and candidate method revisions are compared with frozen baselines under criteria declared in advance.
evidence_items.title: ETALON: Verified Execution and Persistent Research Memory for Agentic Computer-Aided Drug Design

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Well placement decisions are central to field development planning because they require simultaneous consideration of reservoir quality, remaining hydrocarbon potential, subsurface uncertainty, well deliverability, drilling constraints, and development economics. Conventional workflows rely on sequential interpretation and repeated manual screening, which restricts the number of alternatives that multidisciplinary teams can evaluate within a study cycle. Earlier work demonstrated an artificial-intelligence-assisted workflow that combined probabilistic opportunity maps, machine-learning-based target classification, drilling-risk information, completion-quality indicators, and optimization of reservoir targets, well trajectories, and drilling centers. This paper describes the next stage of that work: transformation of the pilot workflow into a scalable, on-premises application integrated with the established subsurface modeling and simulation environment, together with an agentic orchestration layer for broader field-development studies. The productized workflow accepts map-based quality indicators from a deterministic model or an ensemble, enables configurable construction of an opportunity index, excludes existing wells and constrained regions, and uses a development-concept generation engine to place reservoir targets and create drillable trajectories subject to surface no-go areas, existing facilities capacities, and well design constraints. New wells are transferred into simulation cases for performance evaluation with two widely used reservoir simulators. A probabilistic analysis window then compares well-level and development-level outcomes across realizations. At the orchestration level, specialized agents coordinate target identification, trajectory generation, simulation-case preparation, uncertainty evaluation, and scenario ranking while retaining engineer-defined objectives, constraints, review gates, and final approval.
evidence_items.title: From AI Prototype to Agentic AI: Scaling Intelligent Well Placement for Field Development Planning

organizations: Kunlun digital technology, CNPC, Beijing China
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Scientific research in the energy and oil & gas sector faces significant challenges, including massive heterogeneous data, complex mechanisms, high uncertainty, and substantial reliance on expert experience. While recent advancements in generative AI offer autonomy in multi-step reasoning, generic models offered limitations such as hallucinations, insufficient domain knowledge, and poor alignment with researchers' prior works. To address the need for continuity in research trajectories, this study proposes CSTrainer, an ontology-driven, multi-agent system designed for energy-specific scientific research assistance. CSTrainer integrates 5 foundational models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Tencent-Hunyuan, and Doubao-Seed (five foundation LLMs)) and employs a hierarchical architecture featuring multi-agent clusters, cross-model voting, and debate mechanisms. A core innovation is its use of a distributed dynamic ontology framework, which constrains reasoning paths to ensure scientific rigour and mitigate hallucinations. The system facilitates end-to-end research support, encompassing scientific problem formulation, technical route planning, ontology construction, and executable workflow generation, augmented by weighted Bayesian updating and lightweight human-in-the-loop (HIL) feedback. The system was validated on 3 datasets: UNISIM-IV (open), tight gas well re-evaluation (proprietary), and transnational pipeline scheduling (proprietary). Results demonstrate that CSTrainer achieves stable, high quality performance for 3–5 scientific questions extraction, outperforming agent-only baselines by 62.5%–87.5%. While 10 rounds of detailed human feedback yielded optimal results, excessive interaction or scaling beyond 10 problems induced instability. The system attained full marks in the tight gas re-evaluation scenario, confirming its efficacy in bridging the gap between conceptual research and engineering implementation.
evidence_items.title: CSTrainer : An Ontology Driven Multiple AIGC Agentic Approach for Oil and Gas Scientific Research Supporting

evidence_items.summary: Neuraxis evaluates whether a software controller can combine fast admissible-action selection with selective delegation to slower planners. The system couples typed action contracts, a native effect broker, persistent effect records, resource revisions, policy methods, and independent task postconditions. Twelve methods are compared across twenty software-operation families, six variants, and ten seeds, for 14,400 core episodes. Five methods, including a guarded finite-state controller, solve every core episode. The proposed resource-versioned outcome-aware controller M12 solves 1,160 episodes versus 1,200 for the guarded baseline and has higher decision latency. Four component ablations match full M12 task success. A learned routing gate chooses never to defer, and XGBoost exceeds M12 on a small held-out transfer set. A separate post-hoc event audit of 4,320 frozen episodes records 3,915 target-event exposures; M12 selects the scored response more often than M01 but has lower verified task success. This diagnostic does not change the core result or establish a new method. The evidence does not support an M12 success advantage or a measurable task-success contribution from its named components on this suite. The companion task workbench runs bounded file-analysis workflows through a deterministic verified-operation controller; it does not route these tasks through M12. The work contributes a reproducible software-control testbed, an auditable action-execution boundary, and a falsifiable evaluation of fast/slow allocation, together with a negative result identifying benchmark saturation and cancellation handling as central limitations. Source code: CAOS Neuraxis . Data and reproducibility materials are available in the repository's versioned artifacts and validation records.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
evidence_items.title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?

evidence_items.summary: Semantic segmentation of street panoramas can support detailed descriptions of urban environments, yet small datasets and unequal training costs make model selection difficult. This paper documents the two stages of a submission to the PalmCity challenge. In the first stage, nine pretrained segmentation systems are compared using approximately equal computation budgets, and the two leading candidates are trained with three random seeds. An equal probability average of three Encoder only Mask Transformer models with DINOv3 features, evaluated at three image scales with horizontal reflection, reaches 60.95% mean intersection over union on the 84 image validation split and 57.08% on the hidden test leaderboard, first in the snapshot of 5 October 2026. In the second stage, color and crop augmentation, rare class sampling, larger inputs, further architectures, and post processing are tested under the same update budget, and candidates are compared through a paired image bootstrap with selection rules fixed before the results. Training at 768 by 1536 and 896 by 1792 pixels gives the largest gains. The selected ensemble of four models scores 64.53% on validation when trained on the training images alone. Retrained on the training and validation images, it receives 61.54% mean intersection over union and 71.93% mean F1 on the hidden test leaderboard, first among five entries in the snapshot of 30 October 2026. Segment Anything voting, instance mask overlays, and ensembles with other architectures all reduce the validation score. Because the validation images guided many choices and the final models were trained on them, the validation scores are optimistic and the test score is the only independent measurement. The study reports all runs, comparisons, costs, and limits, and releases the code and models.
evidence_items.title: Vision Transformer Ensembles for Panoramic Street Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Infrared multi-frame super-resolution (MFSR) exploits complementary observations to recover spatial detail, but its evaluation remains fragmented across datasets and protocols. A common benchmark is needed to evaluate reconstruction under weak texture, varying thermal contrast, and noise in the source imagery. It should also characterize reconstruction performance across different inter-frame displacement ranges. We introduce IR275K, a curated benchmark containing 594 in- frared video sequences and 275,196 frames. It provides sequence- level train/validation/test splits and a reproducible x4 evaluation protocol. Evaluation spans single-frame and multi-frame recon- struction using seven learned baselines, the CGMamba reference model, and bicubic interpolation. All learned methods are evalu- ated under both bicubic degradation and synthetic mixed sensor noise.EDVRleadstheoverallrankingunderbicubicdegradation, whereas MSDTGP leads under mixed sensor noise. DBSR leads thehigh-displacementUAVsubsetunderbothsettings.Controlled ablations using CGMamba show that real neighboring frames improve PSNR over center-frame repetition by 1.04 dB under bicubic degradation and 0.95 dB under mixed sensor noise. Center-frame conditioning also improves reconstruction under both settings. The benchmark thus reveals how reconstruction rankings and the benefits of neighboring frames depend on evaluation conditions. The complete IR275K dataset is publicly available at: https://github.com/InfraRecon7/IR275K.
evidence_items.title: IR275K: A Benchmark for Infrared Multi-Frame Super-Resolution Toward Efficient Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) perform complex tasks through long-horizon reasoning and tool interaction, where a fundamental trade-off arises between execution efficiency and reasoning robustness. Models at different capability-cost levels offer complementary advantages: lower-cost models enable fast execution but may struggle on difficult reasoning segments, while stronger models provide more robust reasoning at higher computational cost. We present AgentCollab, a self-driven collaborative inference framework that dynamically coordinates models with different reasoning capacities during agent execution. Instead of relying on external routing modules, the framework uses the agent's own self-reflection signal to determine whether the current reasoning trajectory is making meaningful progress, and escalates control to a stronger reasoning tier only when necessary. To further stabilize long-horizon execution, we introduce a difficulty-aware cumulative escalation strategy that allocates additional reasoning budget based on recent failure signals. In our experiments, we instantiate this framework using a two-level small-large model setting. Experiments on diverse multi-step agent benchmarks show that AgentCollab consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier of LLM agents. The code is available at https://github.com/SparkEngineAI/AgentFlashInfer.
evidence_items.title: AgentCollab: A Self-Evaluation-Driven Collaboration Paradigm for Efficient LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Historical map collections are highly diverse in style, scale, and geographic focus, often consisting of many single-sheet documents. Yet most work in map recognition focuses on specialist models tailored to homogeneous map series. In contrast, this article aims to develop generalizable semantic segmentation models and a shared class ontology. We introduce Semap, a new open benchmark dataset comprising 1,439 manually annotated patches designed to reflect the variety of historical map documents. We also evaluate a segmentation workflow that combines procedural data synthesis with multiscale integration. Under the harmonized benchmarks considered here, this workflow attains the strongest performance among the evaluated approaches and viably learns from heterogeneous map data. The results indicate that segmentation performance remains largely stable across map collections, scales, geographic regions, and publication contexts. By providing benchmark data, a shared ontology, and an evaluation of generic segmentation across heterogeneous maps, this work contributes toward integrating the long tail of cartographic archives into historical geographic studies.
evidence_items.title: Generalizable Multiscale Segmentation of Heterogeneous Map Collections

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides the phenotypic and genotypic datasets, analysis scripts, statistical outputs, supplementary documentation, and reproducibility materials associated with the study “Phenotypic differentiation after perenniality-directed selection indicates continued breeding opportunity in diploid-derived perennial sorghum.” The study investigates phenotypic differentiation following perenniality-directed selection in an experimental sorghum breeding population, with particular emphasis on rhizome development and overwinter regrowth. The archived analyses include regression models, hierarchical analyses, sensitivity analyses, genomic assessments, and simulation-based evaluations designed to characterize trait relationships and their implications for perennial sorghum improvement. Version 0.3.1 incorporates reconciled plant-height notation, updated cytotype documentation, and supporting sensitivity analyses. Flow cytometry was conducted on all 75 plants exhibiting overwinter regrowth, of which 72 were classified as diploid and three as tetraploid. A conservative sensitivity analysis excluding eight cytotype-flagged accessions indicated that the principal association between rhizome development and overwinter regrowth remained statistically supported. The repository documents analytical procedures, methodological decisions, and known data-provenance limitations. Genomic findings are interpreted within the context of the same experimental population and should not be considered independent validation of the phenotypic results. Some original historical field records, weather-station source files, and flow-cytometry instrument records were unavailable for independent verification; these limitations are disclosed in the accompanying documentation. The origin of the observed tetraploid individuals remains unresolved.
evidence_items.title: Data and analysis code for "Phenotypic differentiation after perenniality-directed selection indicates continued breeding opportunity in diploid-derived perennial sorghum"

evidence_items.summary: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.
evidence_items.title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science

evidence_items.summary: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. To address this, model embeddings compress each model into a fixed-length vector from which many properties can be predicted. Existing methods, such as EmbedLLM, build these vectors from correctness patterns and question features, and often need large probe batteries to do so. However, many behaviors that are important when choosing a model, such as its verbosity, safety and style, show up more in how it answers than in whether it is correct. We introduce BULLPEN (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings), a framework that extends EmbedLLM in three ways. First, BULLPEN organizes the downstream tasks that prior work uses and adds 20 task benchmarks we built on behavior, style and provenance. Second, it is the first framework to read a model's own answer text jointly with its correctness and the question text. Third, it encodes models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool. Across 260 open-weight models, our answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder. Our encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from only 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute of the full question pool), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83% with the same 400 questions. Because these embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioral auditing and low-cost profiling, and could extend to API-only models. Code and data: https://github.com/wcquesera/bullpen
evidence_items.title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings

evidence_items.summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.
evidence_items.title: TRIDENT and SHAKTI: A Framework and Benchmark for Hindi AI-Text Detection

evidence_items.summary: Although large language models have shown strong capabilities in domain-specific code generation, their performance in robotics software development, especially for the Robot Operating System (ROS), remains largely unexplored. ROS code generation presents distinctive challenges, including complex inter-node coordination, middleware configuration, and lifecycle semantics that go far beyond standard coding benchmarks, and many important correctness properties become observable only once migrated nodes are launched and communicate. We present ROSTrans, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on ROS1-to-ROS2 code migration, a representative and practically important setting for ROS code generation. ROSTrans comprises 108 scaffolded completion tasks drawn from a diverse set of 70+ open-source ROS1 repositories and organized into a hierarchical taxonomy assessing interface-level, behavioral-level and system-level correctness. For every task we establish an executable reference: a verified ROS2 implementation, a runtime test suite that launches the nodes and exercises their topics, services, actions and parameters, and a container ensuring reproducibility. Candidates are scored by injecting only their target files into an otherwise fixed copy of the reference package, so a candidate can neither supply nor weaken the tests it is judged by. Evaluating six frontier LLMs over five stochastic generations per task, we find pass@1 below 10.9%, and that 56.5% of all samples build successfully and then fail at runtime,and 32.0% fail runtime assertions on the migrated interfaces, a class of error no compile-only oracle can detect. Execution-guided repair further improves task success, reaching 49.1% and 47.2% for Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5 after three rounds, respectively.
evidence_items.title: ROSTrans: Empirically Benchmarking LLMs for ROS1-to-ROS2 Migration

evidence_items.summary: When a language model invents a Qur'anic verse or hadith, it gives false authority to text that readers may treat as sacred. Existing Islamic hallucination benchmarks are largely Arabic and often closed-ended, while Bengali resources mainly study general-domain hallucination or factual knowledge. We introduce BILAL-BENCH, a 240-question expert-verified benchmark for open-ended Islamic-source fabrication in Bengali. It covers Qur'anic attribution, hadith, fiqh, contemporary issues, and adversarial false-premise prompts, and uses a two-axis rubric that separates source errors from assertiveness. We evaluate seven open-weight models from 1B to 120B on 1,680 double-annotated responses. Six of the seven models confidently fabricate on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions, with no monotonic improvement from scale. Hadith provenance is the weakest category across models: only two of 315 responses are correct and correctly sourced. The two 8B BanglaLLaMA variants have similar confident-fabrication rates but different error profiles. Models vary far more in whether they withhold a claim they cannot support than in source accuracy: appropriate abstention or false-premise correction ranges from 6 to 46 responses across the benchmark, and does not track parameter count.
evidence_items.title: Do Open Language Models Invent Scripture? BILAL-BENCH: Benchmarking Islamic-Source Fabrication in Bengali

evidence_items.summary: Transcription factors (TFs) play an important role in regulating gene expression, making their identification a fundamental task in computational biology. In this work, we propose GraphTFactor, a novel end-to-end framework that models protein sequences as graphs and directly classifies transcription factors. By encoding sequences into graph structures, the proposed approach naturally handles variable-length inputs while preserving relevant relational information, without imposing length constraints. Experimental results show that GraphTFactor outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of graph-based representations for TF prediction while providing interpretable insights into the sequence regions contributing to the model's predictions. To support reproducibility and practical adoption, we release an open-source software package and an interactive web application that let users easily perform TF prediction on custom sequences.
evidence_items.title: GraphTFactor: A graph-based approach for proteins transcription factor prediction

evidence_items.summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) now underpin critical systems in education, healthcare, and policy advisory contexts, yet remain susceptible to the recursive amplification of bias, misinformation, and error (BME). Feedback loops between user interaction, model retraining, and data reuse accelerate epistemic drift and erode information quality over time. This dissertation presents a standards-aligned governance architecture to detect, quantify, and mitigate these risks across the full AI lifecycle. The research introduces the BME Metric Suite, five original diagnostic metrics: Bias Amplification Rate (BAR), Echo Chamber Propagation Index (ECPI), Information Quality Decay (IQD), Pretraining Diversity Index (PTDI), and Architectural Hallucination Risk Score (AHRS). Empirical validation applied Six Sigma statistical process control (EWMA, CUSUM, and process capability analysis) to a 90-prompt, three-domain factual corpus administered across four evaluation cycles to four frontier architectures (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Grok, and LLaMA 3.1), with a separate multi-turn evaluation comparing natural, engineered, and SymPrompt+ prompting. Results show that drift follows a structured, repeatable pathway; that BAR, ECPI, and IQD operate as an interconnected triad, with PTDI serving as an early-warning signal; that reliability differs substantially across architectures; and that structured prompting modulates conversational behavior without altering underlying architectural signatures. The dissertation operationalizes these diagnostics through the AI Lifecycle Audit and Governance Framework (ALAGF), which combines MIDCOT (Multi-Dataset IQ Drift and Cost Optimization Training) for data governance with SymPrompt+ for oversight of structured human-AI interaction. Tiered escalation (T0 to T5), RACI matrices, and audit evidence packs map the framework to ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23053, ISO 8000, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and the EU AI Act.
evidence_items.title: GOVERNING BME AMPLIFICATION IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: A STANDARDS-ALIGNED FRAMEWORK FOR LLM DATA LIFECYCLE RISK DETECTION AND ETHICAL AI GOVERNANCE

evidence_items.summary: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
evidence_items.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
