evidence_items.summary: A weak answer from a shopping assistant may inconvenience a customer. A weak action from a commerce agent can move money, reserve inventory, change a delivery commitment, or issue a refund. Once an agent can create those effects, the central question is no longer whether its response sounds correct. The question is whether the action is still authorized and commercially valid when the enterprise system commits it. This study introduces a Transaction Control Layer (TCL) that separates an agent's proposal from permission to execute. TCL binds each approved action to grounded intent, delegated authority, current authoritative state, a short validity period, and a stable idempotency key. It then records and reconciles the resulting side effects. We formalize commit validity across five dimensions and define five operational decisions: allow, modify, hold, deny, and escalate. The design is examined with CAV-Bench v1.0.0, an Apache-2.0 reference artifact containing 40 synthetic scenarios and five deterministic architecture profiles. The direct profile reaches an outcome success rate of 0.925, yet only 0.250 of its runs are commit-valid. Adding policy checks, commit-time guards, reconciliation, and lifecycle recovery raises commit-valid success to 0.500, 0.750, 0.875, and 1.000. These values show that the benchmark responds to the controls it was designed to test. They do not estimate real model failure rates or establish production effectiveness. An external replication protocol is therefore included as the next step toward independent validation.
evidence_items.title: A transaction control layer for governed agentic commerce: reference architecture implementation and controlled evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Adaptive prediction intervals can have accurate average coverage while retaining substantial local coverage error. We examine this distinction in a one-step prequential study of fifteen selected time series: eleven generated mechanisms and four real excerpts. The point forecaster is a full-history smoothing-plus-drift adaptation, rather than a native stateful forecaster or the standard finite-history Theta method. Two scale-normalized score-buffer controllers use ACI-style and PID-style updates of an effective miscoverage level. At nominal 80% coverage, their mean rolling absolute coverage errors are 0.0656 and 0.0645, compared with 0.0830 for unadjusted intervals. The substantially smaller errors obtained by first averaging signed coverage deviations over time describe a different statistic and do not establish uniformly accurate local coverage. Every numerical forecast, target, score and controller update is reconstructed and checked against the archived coverage trajectories and final weighted quantile losses. Sensitivity calculations vary nominal coverage, base forecaster, controller gains and generated-series seeds. These selected finite-stream results characterize the evaluated implementations; they provide neither a new coverage theorem nor a general forecasting advantage. Source code, admitted inputs and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS RES ChronoScope . Research atlas: https://chronoscope.fasl-work.com . Not peer reviewed.

evidence_items.summary: Detecting Slowloris Attacks Across Networks — dataset, code and results This record contains the dataset, the code and the results of the article "Detecting Slowloris Attacks Across Networks: Connection-State Features and an Interpretable Fuzzy-Gradient Boosting Detector with Warnings to the Network Administrator", an extended version of our paper presented at the 39th ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC '24). The study evaluates Slowloris detectors on networks not seen during training, using causal timing and connection-state features computed from packet captures and a hybrid detector that combines a fuzzy rule-based classifier tuned by a genetic algorithm (Fuzzy-GA) with gradient boosting. Dataset dados/base unica slowloris v4.csv contains one-second windows from six sources: four captures of our own (an emulated network, a local-area network and two metropolitan-area networks, one of them served over HTTPS) and the Slowloris and slow-body attacks of the CIC-IDS2017 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 datasets. Each window has seven connection-timing features, which also apply to encrypted traffic, ten connection-state features, which describe partial, idle, incomplete and unanswered HTTP connections, and per-window traffic statistics. All features are causal: they use only the packets observed until the end of the window. Each window is labeled by the state of the server (an attack connection occupies the server, with an idle timeout of 120 s) and, for reference, by the share of attack packets. The column captura identifies the source.

evidence_items.summary: Slides for the talk at the 25th International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2026), Bari, Italy, in the workshop “The 21st International Workshop on Ontology Matching”. Entity linking in tables matches short and ambiguous cell mentions to their corresponding knowledge-base entities. Existing approaches typically rely on data preprocessing pipelines that retain either compact or extensive table content as contextual evidence, and then formulate entity linking as a language generation task for instruction-tuned models; recent systems further incorporate explicit reasoning to disambiguate challenging mentions. However, their training supervision is usually static: fixed preference data cannot adapt to the residual errors of an evolving model, while variations in reasoning length can bias sequence-level preference learning. To address these limitations, we present TELLER: Table Entity Linking through Learning from Errors and Reasoning. We first retrieve and rank Wikidata candidates and retain reduced table evidence in the prompt. The direct-answer path applies iterative direct preference optimization and refreshes its preference data with residual errors from the updated model. The reasoning path uses filtered and compressed chain-of-thought rationales for supervised fine-tuning, followed by our iterative length-normalized regularized preference optimization. On the TableInstruct entity-linking subset, the direct-answer path improves accuracy from 94.35\% to 94.50\%; on the MammoTab V2 evaluation set, it improves accuracy from 87.59\% to 88.20\%. The reasoning path improves accuracy from 92.90\% to 92.95\% on TableInstruct and from 79.09\% to 81.85\% on MammoTab V2, while maintaining high rates of complete reasoning generation. These results show that iterative preference learning benefits both concise entity prediction and explicit reasoning.

evidence_items.summary: This paper evaluates the investment performance of the University of Illinois Foundation endowment pool against the benchmark the Foundation designates for itself, over the eleven fiscal years from July 2015 through June 2026. Using public documents, we find that the pool returned 6.94% a year against 9.09% for its benchmark and trailed it in nine of eleven years. Holding gifts and spending fixed, the pool would have been about $771 million (25%) larger on June 30, 2026 had it earned the benchmark return. Roughly 98% of that shortfall accrued in fiscal years 2023–2026, the first four years in which the benchmark  was an investable 70/30 global equity and bond index. Over the ten years through June 2025, the pool also had the lowest return of the 15 Big Ten public pools with a complete record, 6.68% a year against a median of 8.14% for the others, and, over all available years, the lowest estimated alpha after adjusting for exposure to global stock markets. Where the published data permit a decomposition, most of the shortfall arises within asset classes, including manager selection and private investments, rather than from asset allocation. While the Foundation says it does not engage in market timing, its reports also describe shifting money based on market views, and its Form 13F filings show large shifts in the directly held portfolio, from broad index funds to individual stocks and sector funds, and into and out of long-term Treasuries. These patterns are consistent with evidence on the difficulty of identifying superior active managers in advance, and suggest that a low-cost index implementation of the Foundation’s own benchmark would have produced materially better outcomes.

evidence_items.summary: These files contain single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) datasets derived from whole-genome resequencing of 24 Posidonia oceanica samples. Genomic DNA was sequenced using the Illumina platform (150 bp paired-end reads) and aligned against the P. oceanica reference genome Po 2 version 1.0 (NCBI assembly accession GCA 037176725.1). Raw SNP discovery was performed using the snpArcher v1.0 pipeline (https://snparcher.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). Briefly, raw paired-end reads in FASTQ format were adapter-trimmed and quality-filtered with fastp, and the resulting high-quality reads were aligned to the reference genome using BWA-MEM. Duplicate reads were marked with Sambamba markdup prior to variant calling. Variants were initially called independently for each sample in genomic variant call format (gVCF), which retains genotype likelihood information at both variant and reference sites. SNPs and indels were called relative to the reference genome using GATK and an interval-based approach with 50 gVCF intervals, a minimum N-mer size of 500 bp, and diploid genotyping (ploidy = 2). Parameters appropriate for high-coverage sequencing (>10×) were applied (minP = 2, minD = 4), with a heterozygosity prior of 0.005. Callable genomic regions were defined based on mappability using 150-bp k-mers and a minimum mappability score of 1, while coverage-based filtering of callable regions was disabled. Individual gVCFs were then imported into a GenomicsDB datastore and jointly genotyped across all samples to generate a consistent multisample VCF. Variant calls generated across genomic intervals were subsequently concatenated into a genome-wide multisample VCF. During snpArcher post-processing, variants with a minor allele frequency (MAF) <0.01 or >75% missing genotypes were removed. Variant filtering was subsequently conducted with bcftools v1.22 (https://samtools.github.io/bcftools/bcftools.html) using custom parameters to retain high-confidence polymorphisms.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Underwater radiated noise (URN) poses a significant threat to the well-being of marine life from commercial vessels and it is crucial for naval vessels to maintain their stealth capabilities. Hence, the reduction of noise is an actively researched area in the marine sector. The marine propeller, especially when operating in cavitating conditions, contributes 80-85% of the overall URN of the vessel. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with acoustic analogies can predict the propeller noise characteristics in a shorter turnaround time than most other methods. However, an extensive validation is of paramount importance to gain confidence in the simulations. In this work, the propeller from the research vessel Princess Royal is simulated to predict the hydrodynamic (KT, KQ) and hydroacoustic characteristics under cavitating conditions. Extensive test data available from the research work at the University of Newcastle is used to validate the simulation model. Wall modelled large eddy simulation (WMLES) model coupled with the Ffowcs Williams-Hawkings (FWH) acoustics analogy is used for the prediction using the commercial CFD code Simerics-MP. These two simulation techniques were run simultaneously on a 26 million cell mesh. Cavitation was also included in the model using an equilibrium dissolved gas model which captures the evaporation and condensation of the working fluid due to local changes in pressure. These simulations took around 3 hours per complete revolution to run on 192 cores. The binary adaptive meshing technique in Simerics-MP helped to set-up the model in 30 minutes. The CFD results were compared against the test data from a cavitation tunnel experiment[7]. There are also hydrophone measurements available from the tests that were compared with the Computational Hydro-acoustics (CHA) results. Good agreement was found between the test data and simulation results.
evidence_items.title: CFD-Based Hydroacoustic Analysis of a Benchmark Marine Propeller

evidence_items.summary: Aim: To evaluate the occurrence and distribution of microplastics (MPs) in non-edible tissues (gills and digestive tract) and edible tissue (muscle) of Labeo rohita, Cyprinus carpio and Wallago attu. Methodology: Fish specimens were collected bimonthly from October 2024 to March 2025 from the Phillaur and Walipur Kalan stretches of Sutlej River. The collected samples were subsequently processed and analyzed by following the standardized protocol of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Results: Majority of MPs were detected in the intestine (48.0%) and gills (40.4%), whereas lower proportion was found in the muscle tissues (11.6%). The highest level of MP contamination was recorded in W. attu collected from Wallipur Kalan, followed by L. rohita and C. carpio which exhibited moderate levels of contamination. Among different MP shape, fibers were most abundant (58.36%), followed by films (24.21%) and fragments (13.2%). Regarding size distribution, 0.1-0.5 mm MPs were the most prevalent (30.87%), followed by 0.5-1 mm size category (25.18%). In terms of colour, blue MPs were the most abundant (35.48%), followed by transparent (26.33%) and red particles (15.01%). Surface morphological analysis of MPs using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) revealed characteristic weathering features including pits, grooves and cracks. Interpretation: Present findings confirm that widespread occurrence of MPs in commercially important freshwater fish species from the Sutlej River, indicating contamination arising due to anthropogenic activities include direct discharge of plastic waste from industries and domestic source. This highlights the need for improved plastic waste management practices and reduced plastic utilization to mitigate MP pollution in fresh water ecosystems. evidence_items.summary: Abstract Seismic interpretation is rarely a single-task exercise. In practice, an interpreter moves back and forth between data quality, reflector continuity, fault expression, stratigraphic organization, seismic attributes, well control, and geological judgment. A fault cube, a horizon volume, or a conditioned seismic section may each be useful on its own, but none of them is sufficient if the outputs are disconnected from the rest of the interpretation workflow. This paper presents SeismicGen, a framework developed to make seismic AI more reusable and more consistent across interpretation tasks. The workflow is built around a Seismic Foundation Model, or SFM, that provides a shared seismic representation for several specialized interpretation agents. These agents support seismic conditioning, fault characterization, relative geological time estimation, relative acoustic impedance generation, fault and horizon extraction, seismic-to-well tie, and geobody detection. The purpose is not to replace the interpreter with a black-box system, but to provide a common technical layer that helps different AI outputs remain consistent with one another. The workflow starts with seismic preparation, normalization, and quality control. Depending on the interpretation objective, the seismic volume is then passed through selected agents. The outputs are not treated as isolated products. For example, fault probability and displacement indicators can guide fault-surface extraction, while relative geological time can support horizon organization. Results are checked through section-by-section review, geological consistency checks, residual and amplitude analysis, comparison with available well information, and interpreter-led validation. The main practical issue addressed in this paper is the lack of continuity between many existing seismic AI tools. A model may detect faults or pick horizons, but the output often remains separate from the broader interpretation process.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Subsurface Interpretation with Seismic Foundation Models and Agentic Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Production surveillance at fleet scale runs into two constraints. No operations team can review thousands of wells at diagnostic depth every week, and the data for an optimal decision often lives across several source systems. This paper describes a production AI surveillance system built to address these constraints. The system analyzes approximately 6,100 wells each week across four artificial lift types in five operated basins and delivers a prioritized set of recommendations to each engineer. Three concurrent development cycles convert expert diagnostic reasoning into versioned rules, fragmented source data into governed contracts, and engineer corrections that update both the reasoning and the data contracts. The system applies deterministic physics and economic calculations before any AI reasoning. Nodal analysis, production decline evaluation, and lift-specific diagnostics are computed programmatically for the fleet, refreshed on a schedule, and injected into each analysis as governed data. Specialist LLM analyses reason over the evidence without seeing the deterministic conclusions, a synthesis reconciles the two views, and deterministic gates hold correction authority over the output. Engineers individually reviewed more than 950 insights in the first five months. Agreement between engineers and the model exceeded 70 percent across more than 900 reviews that carried a documented reason and a determinable outcome, and it held as the depth of written critiques grew. One in five actioned insights converted to directly confirmed same-well field work within seven days. Twenty-four confirmed-diagnosis wells showed more than 750 BOE/d of combined decline-adjusted improvement. Engineers validate prepared recommendations rather than investigate from scratch. The process was implemented four times, once for each lift method, each build faster and with increased scope over the last, with each lift incorporating its own physics, rules, and source bindings.
evidence_items.title: Physics-Governed Agentic AI for Production Diagnostics: A Transferable Process Validated Across Operational Domains

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reactive shale can swell during contact with water-based drilling fluid, and the resulting LDSM curve is often used to compare models or support drilling decisions. However, many readings from one pellet are still one physical experiment, so a model can look accurate when it is only reconstructing points inside a known curve. This study developed a validation-gated agentic AI workflow and applied it to three source-controlled LDSM records from Talhar, Ranikot, and Khadro shales exposed to the same salt-polymer-glycol Mud A. Each record contained 41 ordered observations over 18 h from a 15 g pellet compacted at 6000 psi for 30 min. Four nonredundant response families and three tree regressors were evaluated. Complete-curve fitting, within-curve interpolation, prediction of the unseen remainder, and 0.5 to 4 h forecasts were tested as separate tasks. Final observed swelling was 4.35% for Talhar, 17.62% for Ranikot, and 5.70% for Khadro. Their average rates at 0.5 h were 6.63, 9.22, and 4.57%/h. Hyperbolic gave the lowest Talhar complete-curve MAE at 0.0750 percentage point, while Weibull gave the lowest Ranikot and Khadro MAEs at 0.0952 and 0.0436 percentage point. Linear interpolation produced lower leave-one-observation-out error than every tree model. The lowest chronological future-block error was still 5.7 to 32.2 times the corresponding interpolation error, showing that accurate reconstruction inside a known curve is not the same as future prediction. The rule-governed agent kept early rate, directly measured swelling, and endpoint-model agreement as separate evidence states. Ranikot reached a high-reactivity screening output at 0.5033 h, Talhar at 5 h, and Khadro reached an elevated-magnitude output at 1.85 h because its initial rate remained below the study-defined 5%/h gate. The workflow completed analytical screening for all three records and routed final fluid selection to matched comparative testing and engineering review.
evidence_items.title: Validation-Gated Agentic AI for Comparative LDSM Shale-Reactivity Assessment and Drilling-Fluid Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Offshore engineering, procurement, construction, and installation work depends on a marine logistics chain capable of balancing urgent construction demand against limited vessel capacity, field-entry and towage approvals, crew compliance, berth congestion, weather windows, fuel and freshwater availability, and cost responsibility across several projects operating on the same island. In many projects, the information needed to make these decisions is scattered across cargo manifests, vessel schedules, permit trackers, daily reports, emails, and spreadsheets. This paper sets out a practical agentic artificial-intelligence control-tower model that brings those fragmented inputs into one predictive and auditable decision environment. Deterministic safety and compliance gates are combined with bounded AI agents covering cargo prioritisation, voyage consolidation, vessel and tug assignment, permit and crew monitoring, weather and berth risk, bunkering forecasts, and project-level cost attribution. The prototype dashboard and workflow were assessed against an anonymised 12-week operating dataset from concurrent offshore construction projects on an ADNOC-operated island in Abu Dhabi. Performance under the observed baseline was compared with a model-assisted re-planning scenario. Average deck-space utilisation rose from 31% to 89%; combined landing-craft productivity increased from about one to 3.2 sailings per week; and completed cargo-barge towage cycles increased from about one to 3.8 cycles per active barge per month. Cargo readiness confirmed before berth booking improved from 57% to 93%, while average berth-related waiting fell from 11.2 to 3.1 hours for each affected voyage. Fuel-allocation completeness increased from 68% to 97%, and daily fuel-forecast error declined from 19.5% to 3.5%. The model also surfaced towage-approval, crew-rotation, weather, berth, and regional-disruption risks before mobilisation.

evidence_items.summary: Multi-hop question answering (MHQA) requires recovering a complete set of supporting documents, yet most retrieval-augmented pipelines apply one evidence budget and one selection strategy to every question. This paper studies benchmark-defined adaptive candidate reranking for Indonesian MHQA in a closed setting in which each question is paired with ten candidate documents. A routing classifier assigns each question to a two-gold-document branch (HotpotQA), processed by two-stage sequential reranking, or to a four-gold-document branch (a bridge-comparison subset of 2WikiMultihopQA), processed by parallel ranking-based reranking, using lightweight XLM-RoBERTa cross-encoders. All components are trained without stemming and selected on a held-out validation split. On 8,000 Indonesian-translated evaluation questions, the framework recovers the complete supporting-document set for 95.40% of questions with 3.00 documents per question and 97.69% document precision. In evidence recovery, it significantly outperforms a single-model fixed-K=4 reranker (+2.60 points; McNemar's exact test p < 10−17); relative to top-4 selection with the same branch-specific scorers, it trades 0.89 points of containment for 23.55 points higher document precision and one document fewer per question. Ablations attribute the largest effect to sequential conditioning (+14.00 points at an equal budget of two documents) and show that routing errors cost 0.03 points within the benchmark, that transfer initialization mainly accelerates convergence, and that Sastrawi stemming degrades the scorers. Class-wise probes and a cross-source test show that the routing classifier relies on a film-topic shortcut and misroutes 10.78% of unseen two-document questions; it is therefore a benchmark-defined controller, not a detector of reasoning complexity, and the results do not establish generalization beyond the evaluated benchmark.

evidence_items.summary: We present a set of six time-temperature (tT) histories, which we refer to as benchmark paths, that can be used as a shared framework for evaluating the sensitivity of a thermochronologic system to the variables inherent in the interpretation of thermochronologic data (e.g., kinetics models, mineral compositions or geometries, etc.). These benchmark paths span 100 Myr, include monotonic and nonmonotonic histories that represent plausible geologic scenarios, and have a range of cooling rates through different chronometer partial retention/annealing temperatures. Here, we demonstrate their utility by presenting a method for “tuning” these paths to 11 different kinetics models for the apatite (U-Th-Sm)/He (n=5), apatite fission-track (n=2), and zircon (U-Th)/He (n=4) systems. These tuned tT paths provide a practical comparison of the kinetics models for each system and the data patterns they predict, thereby offering anyone performing thermal history analysis the ability to consider how their choice of kinetics model may impact their data interpretation. The adoption of benchmark paths for evaluating kinetics models and other variables provides a practical way to evaluate and communicate the decisionmaking processes that are inherent in thermochronologic modeling and data interpretation.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for mental health support, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on supportive capabilities rather than whether models consistently adhere to professional ethical boundaries. This issue is particularly important in multi-turn interactions, where users may introduce new information or exert emotional pressure over time. We introduce MindEth-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating ethical boundary adherence in multi-turn mental health interactions. Grounded in professional ethical standards for mental health services in China, MindEth-Bench covers multiple dimensions of ethical conduct and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to systematically explore interaction trajectories that stress-test model boundaries. Experiments across nine LLMs show that models that initially respond appropriately can shift toward ethical violations over extended interactions, with substantial variation across models and ethical dimensions. evidence_items.summary: Agent runtimes that plan before acting run every step as soon as it is ready. Neither these runtimes nor their benchmarks distinguish a step that is ready from a step the request needs, and the difference is large: across 303 requests on 154 production workflows, an eager runtime that stops once the goal is met spends 62.2% of its CPU on work the request never needed. LazyAgent is, to our knowledge, the first complete formulation of demand-driven execution for agent runtimes. Its rule: run a ready step only if the current request needs it, and keep that answer exact as the plan changes. A demanded set derived from the program decides, in one traversal with no model calls, so LazyAgent spends nothing outside the request. Because demand is defined exactly, its behavior is proved: builders know before any run where demand must save and where it must tie. The bill is known before a plan runs, so LazyAgent can act as a query optimizer to choose among candidate workflows. Measured live against that eager runtime, LazyAgent saves 51.7% and 52.1% of container time on release gates where a frontier LLM writes the patches, 12.8% of tokens on DataSciBench plans at matched quality, and 24.0% of dollars inside a live LangGraph application, with no losses. When the LLM re-plans after real code failures, it solves every solvable goal with 11.7% fewer tokens per goal. On the production workflows it saves 42.0% of CPU, ties exactly where a request needs the whole graph, and adds at most 0.43% overhead. The same set steers every physical operation: projection saves 80-89% of a shared CI step, where the identical eager control saves 0.0%. Public agent benchmarks are designed the same way as eager runtimes, so they cannot show this difference. We compose our test programs from their tasks and call on industry to build benchmarks that measure how efficiently agent workflows run.
evidence_items.title: LazyAgent: Demand-Driven Materialization and Physical Optimization of Agentic Programs

evidence_items.summary: In the US, 67% of children aged 9 to 17 have used AI chatbots. To our knowledge, no large-scale open benchmark measures, with a graded standard of response quality, how safely language models handle child-specific risks across multi-turn conversations and age groups. We introduce KORA Bench, an open benchmark for child safety in language-model interactions. For this, we build 737 child-risk scenarios and run each one across 30 models from 9 providers under two prompting conditions. This produces 44,220 simulated multi-turn conversations. The scenarios cover 25 risks in 8 categories, developed with input from more than 20 experts and research groups in child safety. A three-level grading scale rates each conversation as failing, adequate, or exemplary. It measures not only whether a model avoids harm in these scenarios, but the quality of the response. Averaged across the 30 models, the default-condition score is 44.7%, below the all-adequate baseline of 50%. Scores range from 10% to 76%. Three results stand out. First, educational and epistemic integrity is the weakest category, at 25.6% on average. Second, a detailed child-aware safety prompt raises scores by 24.8 percentage points on average across all 30 models. Third, among the three behaviors we score, how often a model redirects a child to a trusted adult is the one most strongly associated with overall safety, an exploratory finding subject to a common-method caveat. Across the benchmark, the two lowest-scoring individual risks are academic dishonesty at 16% and cognitive atrophy at 15%. Two external review studies suggest the judge is conservative relative to the review protocols we used. Agreement is moderate (weighted κ = 0.52 on the valid subset), so the absolute scores need care. Code, prompts, and scenarios are released at https://github.com/korabench/benchmark (tag 1.0.0).

evidence_items.summary: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. evidence_items.summary: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
evidence_items.title: Confident Fools or Careful Searchers? A Behavioural Study of When LLMs Search Beyond Their Static Internal Memory

evidence_items.summary: Image composition labels such as center, diagonal, or rule of thirds describe visual structure rather than object categories. We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence benchmark for photographic composition. Given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain why the label applies. KU-PCPE contains 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. evidence_items.summary: Keystroke dynamics---the timing of a person's key presses and releases---is a low-cost, non-intrusive behavioral biometric. However, public benchmarks and most empirical evidence focus on typing in Latin scripts, predominantly English, and do not cover speakers of Ge'ez-script (Ethiopic) languages such as Amharic, which has more than 35 million native speakers. Ethiopic syllabic characters are commonly entered through multi-key transliteration, creating different motor-planning demands. This raises the question of whether timing-based verification methods developed for Latin scripts transfer effectively to other writing systems. We present and characterize a keystroke dynamics corpus collected from a shared pool of typists completing three text-entry tasks---fixed text, free text, and password entry---in Amharic and English. The corpus contains 114,955 labeled keystroke events across five sub-corpora (4,751--51,813 rows each), with up to 25 raw and derived timing fields per event. We report a systematic exploratory data analysis (EDA) covering structural composition; missingness and duplication; demographic and skill-level coverage; univariate and bivariate timing distributions; feature redundancy (correlation and hierarchical clustering); per-user sample imbalance; and user distinguishability in Principal Component Analysis (PCA), t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) projections. The analysis finds strongly right-skewed timing features, a small number of algebraically redundant feature pairs, a coefficient of variation in per-user sample counts of up to 2.4, and substantial visual overlap between users in low-dimensional projections. Together, these properties plausibly explain the 40--60% rank-1 accuracy and 10--20% equal error rate (EER) previously obtained with baseline classifiers on this cohort.
evidence_items.title: Typing Rhythms Beyond the Latin Script: An Amharic–English Keystroke Dynamics Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.
evidence_items.title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.
evidence_items.title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World

evidence_items.summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) aims to recover well-exposed and perceptually faithful images from severely degraded observations. Recent diffusion-based generative methods achieve strong perceptual quality by leveraging powerful image priors, but their iterative sampling incurs substantial computational cost, limiting practical deployment. Despite recent efficiency gains in generative LLIE, high-quality enhancement with a single function evaluation and low overall computation remains challenging, particularly under diverse real-world low-light conditions. We introduce GLOW-FM, a one-step latent flow-matching framework for efficient generative LLIE. GLOW-FM performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE and leverages Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to enable enhancement with a single function evaluation. Matched comparisons with alternative one-step objectives support TVM as an effective design choice, and, to the best of our knowledge, this is its first adaptation to image restoration and specifically to LLIE. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that GLOW-FM achieves competitive image quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization while requiring only a single function evaluation and 34 GFLOPs for the small variant. These findings highlight the potential of GLOW-FM to bring generative LLIE closer to practical deployment through single-step inference and compact latent modeling. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.
evidence_items.title: GLOW-FM: Efficient Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement with One-Step Latent Flow Matching

evidence_items.summary: Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a critical tumor suppressor whose dysregulation is frequently implicated in cancer progression. This study reports the synthesis and structural characterization of a new series of cationic quaternary ammonium compounds, specifically 1,3-diaryl-3-hydroxy-2,3,6,7-tetrahydro-5H-imidazo[2,1-b][1,3]thiazin-1-ium bromides, designed as potential PP2A activators. The chemical structures were confirmed using 1H NMR, 13C NMR, IR, LC-MS, and elemental analysis. Spectroscopic data, including 1H NMR, show a characteristic AB-type spin system at 4.33–4.53 ppm with coupling constants J = 12.1–12.5 Hz, and 13C NMR signals at 93.9–94.3 ppm for C-OH, revealing that these compounds exist in a stable bicyclic tautomeric form. Preliminary screening identified compounds 9L and 9C, which statistically significantly increased PP2A activity. In vitro pharmacological screening against 60 human cancer cell lines (NCI-60) demonstrated broad-spectrum anticancer activity. Notably, derivative 9L (1-(4-ethylphenyl)-3-(4-cyclohexylphenyl)-3-hydroxy-2,3,6,7-tetrahydro-5H-imidazo[2,1-b][1,3]thia­zin-1-ium bromide) exhibited potent growth inhibition across all tested lines, with significant lethality observed in leukemia and small cell lung cancer cells. Molecular docking studies using the Yasara-Vina evolutionary algorithm and chemPLP in DataWarrior against the PP2A core (PDB ID: 2IE4) identified high binding affinities (up to –7.99 kcal/mol for 9L in Vina and -65,731 Docking Score for chemPLP). These results suggest that this class of imidazo-thiazines is a promising scaffold for developing new anticancer agents by pharmacologically modulating PP2A. suppl.zip - all docking files supplementary.pdf - analysis of structure results

evidence_items.summary: The early diagnosis of the vehicle malfunctions by the artificial intelligence (AI) is a promising way to reduce the breakdowns and the maintenance cost, but the reported accuracies in the literature are usually very high and they may not reflect the real use. In this paper, six machine learning classifiers were trained on the public Engine Fault DB dataset, which contains 55,999 records of 14 engine and exhaust variables under one normal and three fault conditions. The models were evaluated by two protocols, a random five-fold split and a blocked split in which the test segments represent unseen operating conditions. In addition, a random-effects meta-analysis of nine published studies was conducted. The results showed that the four-class accuracy was about 75% under the random split, and it dropped to between 41.17% and 66.92% under the blocked split. However, the detection of the fault against the normal state was almost perfect (AUC = 1.000), and when the two fault types which cannot be separated were merged, the accuracy became 98.22% with all the signals and 97.34% with six on-board signals only. The meta-analysis gave a pooled reported accuracy of 96.50% (95% CI 92.63% to 98.38%) with a very high heterogeneity (I2 = 98.47%). The findings indicate that, on this dataset, the AI models can detect the presence of a fault reliably, while the isolation of the fault type under new operating conditions remains difficult and it needs a stricter validation practice.

evidence_items.summary: Against the backdrop of policies promoting quality enhancement and excellence in vocational education alongside educational evaluation reforms, traditional classroom teaching assessments struggle to comprehensively reflect teaching quality due to limitations such as single-dimensional data and insufficient technological empowerment. To address this, this study constructs an AI-driven multimodal data fusion model for classroom teaching evaluation. This model encompasses a five-layer technical architecture—data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, metric calculation, and result feedback—integrating three types of multi-source heterogeneous information: teaching behavior data (based on DBSCAN clustering analysis), physiological state data (combined with ResNet-18 emotion recognition), and dynamic effect data (using TransE knowledge transfer evaluation). This enables comprehensive and precise diagnosis of the classroom teaching process. Empirical validation was conducted in smart classroom environments using S-T behavioral analysis, engagement curves, and the Rt-Ch model. Results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in identifying critical issues such as imbalanced teaching pacing and fluctuating student engagement, significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness and objectivity of evaluations. This research not only provides a replicable technical pathway for diagnosing vocational education classroom quality but also offers theoretical support and practical examples for the deep integration of artificial intelligence and educational assessment.
evidence_items.title: Construction and Empirical Research on Classroom Teaching Evaluation Model of Vocational Education Based on Artificial Intelligence Multimodal Data Fusion

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) — systems of autonomous, goal-directed software agents that plan, act, and coordinate with reduced human oversight — is moving from research prototypes toward applied data-science, perception, and decision-support pipelines. Yet the literature remains fragmented across largely disconnected strands: trust-aware orchestration of multimodal agents for visual classification, human adoption of autonomous AI agents, automated machine-learning (AutoML) pipelines for tabular data, and fully autonomous multi-agent systems for end-to-end data engineering. This review synthesizes four recent studies spanning these strands, together with the broader literature on multi-agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), large-language-model (LLM)-based knowledge-graph construction, and explainable AI, to build a unified picture of agentic AI as applied to intelligent data science. We propose a four-part taxonomy — perception-level trust orchestration, human adoption of agentic systems, automated feature/model pipelines, and autonomous data-engineering agents — and compare the reviewed studies on automation level, reasoning mechanism, knowledge representation, retrieval use, trust treatment, and evaluation methodology. The synthesis shows that individual components of an agentic data-science stack (confidence calibration, retrieval-grounded re-evaluation, automated feature synthesis, autonomous pipeline repair) have each demonstrated measurable gains in isolation, but no reviewed system couples them with a persistent, multimodal knowledge-graph layer, and adoption research indicates that user trust is not the dominant driver of usage intention — a finding with direct design implications.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Systems: A Review of Multi-Agent Reasoning, Trust, Orchestration, and Autonomous Data Science

evidence_items.summary: This article investigates the communicative functions of irony in English and Uzbek from a contrastive-pragmatic perspective. Irony is approached as a complex pragmatic phenomenon arising from the incongruity between the literal content of an utterance and the speaker’s intended communicative meaning, with contextual interpretation and implicit evaluation playing a central role. The study aims to identify the principal communicative functions of irony, describe their realization in English and Uzbek, and establish their shared and language-specific features. The research draws on contrastive, contextual, linguopragmatic, and semantic-pragmatic methods. Based on theoretical sources and constructed illustrative examples, the article examines the critical-evaluative, humorous, emotional-expressive, indirect-communicative, social-regulatory, and interpersonal-management functions of irony. The analysis suggests that irony is not limited to conveying a meaning opposite to the literal content of an utterance.
evidence_items.title: COMMUNICATIVE FUNCTIONS OF IRONY IN ENGLISH AND UZBEK

evidence_items.summary: The valorization of biomass and its transformation into fuels are highly interesting due to the abundance of biomass and its almost neutral carbon emissions. In this article, we show the production of γ-valerolactone (GVL), a valuable product, from furfural (FF), a compound that can be easily obtained from biomass. This FF to GVL transformation involves a catalytic cascade reaction with two hydrogenation steps. Pt and/or Zr supported on sepiolite catalysts have been prepared and tested in the FF transformation reaction. A physical mixture of a Zr-based and a Pt-based catalyst has reached a yield to GVL of ca. 50% after 16 h at 180 ° C. This performance largely exceeds that obtained by each of the single Pt or single Zr metal catalysts independently, showing a strong synergistic effect. These data suggest that each metal (Pt and Zr) plays an important and complementary role in different reaction steps. Furthermore, the physical mixture appears to be much more efficient than bimetallic Pt/Zr catalysts synthesized with the same amount of metals. The role of the type of acidity and the oxidation state of the surface platinum species on the catalytic performance has been discussed. Moreover, this reaction has been carried out in batch and continuous flow reactors, and a comparative study between the two operation modes has been undertaken. A certain correlation between the catalytic results obtained by both operation modes has been found. Description of methods used for collection/generation of data:  Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of catalysts were collected between 10 and 80 ° at 2θ using an Enraf Nonius FR590 sealed tube diffractometer (Bruker, Delft, The Netherlands) equipped with a monochromatic Cu Kα1 source (40 kV and 30 mA).

evidence_items.summary: This study examines the impact of credit portfolio diversification on bank profitability, with a specific focus on the moderating role of bank size in ASEAN commercial banks. Using a panel dataset comprising 56 banks across six ASEAN countries from 2017 to 2023, the research applies a random effects panel regression model to analyze the effect of credit concentration, measured by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), on Return on Assets (ROA). The results reveal a significant negative relationship between HHI and ROA, indicating that higher diversification enhances profitability. Additionally, the interaction between HHI and bank size (measured by the logarithm of total assets) is negative and significant, suggesting that the positive effect of diversification weakens as bank size increases. These findings are robust across multiple model specifications and control variables, including capital adequacy, credit risk, liquidity, inflation, GDP growth, and state ownership. The study highlights the nuanced dynamics between diversification and institutional scale and provides implications for both banking strategy and regulatory policy. It recommends size-sensitive diversification approaches and capital management strategies to maximize performance outcomes in the ASEAN banking sector.
evidence_items.title: THE ROLE OF BANK SIZE IN MODERATING THE IMPACT OF CREDIT PORTFOLIO DIVERSIFICATION ON BANK PROFITABILITY IN ASEAN

evidence_items.summary: Zinc oxide nanostructured electrodes were successfully synthesized by a simple method of anodization in different aqueous bicarbonate electrolytes. The influence of the anodization electrolyte composition (by adding ethanol or glycerol) on the morphology and the photoelectrocatalytic properties of the zinc oxide electrodes was studied, as well as the combined effect of anodizing under controlled hydrodynamic conditions . Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope (FE-SEM) images of the ZnO electrodes showed that the addition of ethanol or glycerol to the anodization electrolyte resulted in changes in size and morphology of the nanostructures . Thus, ZnO nanowires, nanotubes , nanosponge and nanospheres were obtained. Additionally, multi-factor analysis of the variance (ANOVA) revealed that photocurrent density response during water splitting test experimented significant variations depending on the anodization electrolyte composition. In particular, the best photoelectrochemical performance was achieved for the ZnO nanostructures anodized in low amounts of ethanol or glycerol. Description of methods used for collection/generation of data:  Anodization was performed using a zinc rod (99,999% purity/ 8 mm in diameter) as the working electrode and a platinum foil (1 cm2) as the counter electrode. Previously to anodization, the surface of the zinc rod was abraded with 240–4000 SiC paper to obtain a mirror finish, degreased by sonication in ethanol and dried in air. Subsequently, the zinc rod was covered by Teflon to exclusively expose 0.5 cm2 to the electrolyte. Then, anodization was performed at 10 V for 10 min in a 50 mM NaHCO3 aqueous electrolyte with different ethanol or glycerol amounts (10, 25 and 50% v/v). Conductivity of the fresh electrolytes was measured prior to anodization using a conductimeter (CRISON BASIC 30).
evidence_items.title: Control on the morphology and photoelectrocatalytic properties of ZnO [Dataset]

evidence_items.summary: Data and notebooks of work package 3 (WP3, formulation and algorithms ) of CERTA (Certified, Embedded, Risk-aware Test design for Analog circuits), by Telmo Miguel-Medina. CERTA designs the self-test of board-level analog circuits: which nodes, stimuli and readings an embedded test should use so that the diagnostic coverage required by IEC 61508 or ISO 26262 is reached, and certified with a confidence interval, at the lowest hardware cost. WP3 formulated that problem and solved it. This deposit holds everything WP3 produced: - the cost and instrument model of a microcontroller (STM32G474) applied to the benchmark circuits, with the assumed prices of the parts a plan adds; - the failure rate, severity weight and IEC and ISO classes of 537 faults, from MIL-HDBK-217F Notice 2 and MIL-HDBK-338B; - the 21 result tables of nine notebooks: risk-weighted coverage and its certification by weighted fault sampling, the greedy and its Pareto front, the exact optimum by integer linear programming, the theoretical bound from the sensitivity matrix and its ambiguity groups, and experiments E2 (greedy against the optimum), E3 (joint against sequential design) and E4 (plans chosen with and without risk weighting on three application cases); - the notebooks that produced every table, executed and with their figures, and the two modules that define the benchmark and the cases as selection problems; - the report of milestone G3, which summarises the results and the decision taken on them.
evidence_items.title: CERTA · WP3 data: minimum-cost self-test design with embedded cost, fault priors and an exact optimum.

evidence_items.summary: Background: Lead poisoning remains a significant global public health concern because of its widespread environmental distribution, occupational exposure and persistent toxic effects on multiple organ systems. Lead is a cumulative toxic metal that primarily affects the nervous, haematological, renal, cardiovascular and reproductive systems. Children are particularly vulnerable because of their developing nervous systems and greater gastrointestinal absorption of lead. Although prevention and elimination of exposure are the primary approaches to management, chelation therapy plays an important role in patients with significantly elevated blood lead concentrations or severe clinical manifestations. Objective: This review examines the pharmacological mechanisms of chelation therapy in lead poisoning, evaluates the clinical applications and limitations of currently available chelating agents, and discusses emerging therapeutic approaches and future research directions. Methods: A narrative literature review was developed using published scientific literature, clinical studies, toxicological reviews and international clinical guidelines. Particular emphasis was placed on the pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic efficacy, safety profiles and clinical applications of dimercaprol, calcium disodium EDTA, succimer and D-penicillamine. Results: Chelating agents reduce the biologically available lead burden by forming stable metal–ligand complexes that facilitate elimination, predominantly through renal excretion. Succimer is commonly used in selected patients with moderate lead poisoning, whereas calcium disodium EDTA and dimercaprol have important applications in severe poisoning and lead encephalopathy. However, clinical evidence indicates that reducing blood lead concentrations does not necessarily reverse established neurological injury.
evidence_items.title: Chelation therapy in lead poisoning: pharmacological mechanisms, clinical applications and emerging therapeutic approaches

evidence_items.summary: The InvigoratEU External Influence Index is a structured empirical instrument developed within the Horizon Europe–funded InvigoratEU project to systematically assess and compare the political-security, economic, and societal influence of major external actors in the EU’s Neighbourhood. The Index underpins four key project deliverables, including the Long Policy Reports on Russia, China, and Turkey, as well as the forward-looking scenario analysis on foreign interference until 2035. It is applied across nine EU (potential) candidate countries in the Western Balkans and the Eastern Trio (Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Ukraine). Conceptually, the Index draws on established theoretical frameworks, including the distinction between linkages and leverage, the notion of soft power, and a tripartite classification of external influence across political-security, economic, and societal domains. These conceptual foundations are translated into a structured and operationalised measurement framework composed of clearly defined indicators and weighted dimensions. Methodologically, the index relies on a mixed-methods approach combining desk research, structured scoring based on publicly available data and expert assessments, and semi-structured interviews. The scoring system operates on a 0–3 scale and is rescaled to a 0–10 range for comparative clarity, enabling both cross-country and longitudinal analysis across benchmark years (2013, 2018, and 2023). By providing a transparent, replicable, and comparative framework, the InvigoratEU External Influence Index contributes to a more systematic understanding of how external actors shape political, economic, and societal developments in EU (potential) candidate countries.
evidence_items.title: InvigoratEU External Influence Index

evidence_items.summary: This paper proposes a risk-averse self-scheduling framework for a hybrid wind–battery power plant (HPP) participating in the day-ahead (DA) market while accounting for battery degradation costs. The problem is modeled as a stochastic mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that seeks to maximize the expected profit. The uncertainty sources are wind generation and market prices. Battery degradation has been integrated into the optimization problem as a function of the energy throughput. To address the economic risk associated with market prices and renewable generation uncertainties, two risk management approaches are investigated: Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and second-order stochastic dominance (SOSD) constraints. A feasible benchmark region is identified to guarantee the feasibility of the SOSD-constrained problem. Numerical results demonstrate that SOSD constraints enable controlling the lowest profit compared to conventional CVaRbased risk management and provide more flexibility in the profit distribution. In addition, neglecting the battery degradation affects the profit significantly.
evidence_items.title: Risk-Averse Self-Scheduling of a Hybrid Wind–Battery Power Plant in the Day-Ahead Market Considering Battery Degradation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This paper proposes a multiagent large language model (LLM)–based system for early-stage building layout planning, which enables flexible design requirement inputs and robust spatial reasoning. Existing generative methods often depend on structured inputs, and perform poorly when faced with incomplete requirements or regulatory constraints. Moreover, although LLMs excel at understanding language, they typically lack the spatial reasoning capabilities required for layout generation. To address these limitations, the proposed system includes five core modules: a requirement interpreter that standardizes design requirements and employs multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to fetch similar layouts; a planner module composed of specialized LLM agents such as an architect, accessibility expert, and user experience advocate; a layout executor that transforms planning strategies into bubble diagrams; and an evaluation module that combines rule-based checks and LLM-based feedback. All modules are coordinated by a director module using multichain-of-thought reasoning to iteratively refine the design process. The system supports natural language prompts, layout boundaries, and optional reference layouts, making it suitable for both incomplete and detailed design scenarios. After a bubble diagram is finalized, a diffusion-based generative model produces a complete architectural layout. Experimental results using the Tell2Design data set demonstrated significant improvements in both geometric quality and semantic alignment over a baseline LLM-only system. Case studies of office and multiapartment buildings further validated the system’s adaptability and effectiveness in complex design contexts.
evidence_items.title: A Multiagent Large Language Model–Based System for Early-Stage Building Layout Planning

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of healthcare through tools that help organise medical information, support clinical decisions, answer common questions, and improve communication. These changes affect more than treatment and efficiency: they can also influence how patients feel, how much they trust healthcare professionals, and whether they feel heard and respected. This paper reviews AI in patient–healthcare relationships from a psychosocial perspective. It considers trust, empathy, privacy, patient autonomy, health literacy, anxiety, accessibility, and the role of clinicians in explaining AI-supported decisions. AI can make some services faster and easier to access, but it may also create distance when communication feels automated or when recommendations are difficult to understand. The paper argues that AI should strengthen—not replace—the human relationship at the centre of care. Responsible use requires transparency, protection of personal information, inclusive design, careful evaluation, and meaningful human oversight..

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The paper investigates the turbulent flow generated by a wall jet. A numerical benchmark of six turbulence closures including two-equation and seven-equation models in their high- or low-Reynolds number formulations, is performed. The Standard k - ε , Realizable k - ε , k - ω SST, the linear and quadratic pressure-strain Reynolds Stress Models (RSM) and RSM based on ω available within Ansys Fluent 2023R2 and OpenFOAM v11 are systematically compared with reference experimental data available from the literature for the jet Reynolds number of R e j = 9,600 . Generally, the specific dissipation rate ω appears to be a better candidate than ε to determine the length scale of the turbulence for this particular configuration. Thus, the k - ω SST and RSM- ω models perform better than the others to predict the wall jet spreading rate, maximum Reynolds number or friction coefficient. The linear pressure-strain RSM fails to predict the mean streamwise velocity profile, exhibiting a large deficit in the log region. A budget analysis of the turbulence kinetic energy transport equation is also performed for the low-Reynolds number models. The intriguing behavior of the linear pressure-strain RSM is confirmed by the production term’s profile, which peaks earlier than the other models at about y + ≃ 5 . Overall, the k - ω SST model can be recommended because it offers a good trade-off between accuracy and computational efforts.

evidence_items.summary: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new paradigm that allows intelligent systems to behave independently, pursue specific objectives, and adapt to changing circumstances. Agentic AI combines reasoning, planning, memory, learning, and tool utilization to do complicated tasks with minimal human involvement, in contrast to traditional AI systems that mainly react to user inputs. In this article, takes a look at Agentic AI from every angle: its theoretical underpinnings, technological supports, architectural blueprints, and real-world uses. Many models and frameworks are covered, including cognitive and modular designs, systems based on reinforcement learning, hybrid models, and multi-agent systems. Symbolic, probabilistic, and self-reflective reasoning are some of the reasoning methodologies covered. Classical, hierarchical, and adaptive planning strategies are also covered. Agents' ability to reliably and efficiently execute tasks is investigated by looking at memory management, communication protocols, coordination mechanisms, and collaborative decision-making. A wide range of business, medical, financial, academic, and personal aid apps are evaluated in the poll. Privacy, security, computational costs, scalability, and unexpected behavior are the main issues that are highlighted in the end. The study emphasizes the need for more investigation into how to create Agentic AI systems that are reliable, flexible, and effective.

evidence_items.summary: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the training-inference mismatch between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a numerical discrepancy of the engine and a policy lag of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.
evidence_items.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling

evidence_items.summary: In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R^2Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R^2Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. evidence_items.summary: Fraudulent banking operations bring several problems related to financial safety, reliability of operations, and risk management. The goal of this research is to detect fraudulent operations in banks applying artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques. The methodology includes data preprocessing of banking transactions, missing values' imputation, encoding of categorical features, normalization of numerical features, and random under sampling due to class imbalance problem. Transaction features such as transaction amount, account balance, transaction type, geographical location, transaction frequency, and history of fraud detection are used to discover possible frauds. Machine learning classifiers are used to differentiate between normal operations and fraudulent transactions. The innovation consists in combining transaction-related behavioral characteristics, class imbalance handling, and classifier comparison in fraud recognition framework. There are 50,000 samples in the dataset; among them, there are 47,573 normal transactions, 2,423 fraud transactions, and four samples having no fraud label. According to the given confusion matrix, the framework demonstrates 98.33% accuracy, 98.66% precision, 98.00% recall, and 98.33% F1-score. It proves good classification results for fraud recognition tasks. To get actual values of ROC and AUC, predictions must be calculated for various classification thresholds.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping teaching, learning, and research by offering tools that can support educational practice and academic work. This paper examines AI applications in education, their potential benefits, associated challenges, and ethical implications. It considers how AI can assist teachers with lesson planning, instructional materials, assessment, and feedback; support students through personalized learning and explanations of academic concepts; and help researchers with literature searches, data analysis, reference organization, and academic writing. Drawing on a review of existing literature, the paper identifies opportunities to improve educational efficiency, accessibility, and academic productivity. It also highlights concerns involving data privacy, algorithmic bias, inaccurate outputs, academic dishonesty, unequal access to technology, and overdependence on AI tools. The literature points to the importance of user training, ethical guidelines, institutional support, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content (Maphalala & Ajani, 2025; Khatri & Karki, 2023). The paper argues that AI should complement—not replace—teachers, learners, and researchers. Responsible integration requires a balance between technological innovation and human judgment, creativity, critical thinking, and academic integrity.

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning models for mapping heavy metal concentrations in soil are becoming increasingly popular for making decisions regarding which areas to remediate. However, the reported accuracies of these models are typically based upon the same set of clustered samples that were used to create the model. In this study, we use a controlled simulation to determine how reliable the reported accuracies are and what the implications are for remediation decisions. Twenty synthetic lead contaminated sites (each 100 x 100 grid) were created with known concentrations in each cell. Each site was then sampled using preferential clustered sampling methods to obtain 300 laboratory samples. Eight different model configurations were evaluated using both random and spatial-block cross-validation against a complete census of all un-sampled cells. Random cross-validation overestimated the census R2 for 19 out of 20 sites (mean 0.86 vs. 0.74), while spatial-block cross-validation was pessimistic (0.66). Prediction intervals calibrated using random residuals provided 82% coverage at a nominal 90%, and 64% outside of the area of applicability; spatial-block calibration provided 94% and 84%. By treating each prediction as a probability and applying a cost-ratio rule, we were able to reduce missed exceedances from 31% to 5% at a miss-to-false-alarm cost ratio of 10. Additional space-filling sampling resulted in the lowest map error, while preferential and uncertainty-driven sampling resulted in the highest recall of contaminated cells. Models developed solely from spectral proxies did not transfer well to new sites. These results suggest that reporting accuracy under multiple validation schemes, utilizing uncertainty-aware decision rules, and clearly defining the limits of applicability will improve decision-making. All findings are simulation-based and will need to be verified with field data.
evidence_items.title: Validation-Aware AI for Soil Contamination Assessment and Remediation

evidence_items.summary: Background: DUWLs easily become colonized by microorganisms due to narrow tubing, intermittent flow, and stagnation allowing adhesion and biofilm formation to occur. Patients and dental health-care workers are potentially at risk of exposure to microorganisms during procedures if contaminated outlet water is present. Objectives: The aim of this study was to assess the microbial contamination, biofilm formation and waterline hygiene-related parameters in governmental and private dental clinics. Methods: This study was comparative cross sectional laboratory study carried out at Al-Hilla Surgical Teaching Hospital and clinics from 2/1/2026 to 30/5/2026. 60 dental units were involved in the study (30 governmental and 30 private dental units). Two hundred and forty (240) water samples were taken from air-water syringes, high-speed handpiece lines, cup fillers and source water/reservoir bottles. The culture-based heterotrophic plate counts were done and reported as CFUs/mL. Conventional microbiological and biochemical tests were used for the identification of isolates and selected bacteria were evaluated for the ability to form biofilms using the microtiter plate method. Results: The median heterotrophic counts were higher in governmental clinic than in the private clinic (1200 vs. 430 CFU/mL, p<0.001). The overall prevalence rate was 54.2% with more in governmental than in private clinics (70.0% vs. 38.3%, p<0.001). Lines using high speed handpieces were the most contaminated. Flushing decreased the median counts from 920 to 380CFU/mL with 35.0% still being unacceptable (p<0.001). Of the isolates tested, 55.0% had moderate or strong biofilm production and there was a positive correlation with CFU/mL (rho=0.58, p<0.001). The independent risk factors were lack of disinfection, lack of filtration, lack of flushing and the age of the unit (> 5 years).
evidence_items.title: Comparative Culture-Based Evaluation of Dental Unit Waterline Biofilm Contamination
